name: Sara Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We grow vegetables for two supermarkets: leeks, cabbages, broccoli and carrots, about four hundred acres, plus some beef cattle on the grass we rest between crops. Right now it's leeks and cabbages, so at six I'm in the pack-house, which is the big shed where the veg gets trimmed, washed and bagged. I check the orders that came in overnight from the supermarket, and they change every single day. Then I'm out to the field to see the cutting gang.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a field of cabbages on a frosty morning, all in rows, every one the same size, knowing it's sold before it's cut. What wears me out is the supermarket ringing at four in the afternoon to cut tomorrow's order by a third. We've cut the veg already. It goes to the cattle or the bin.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Pete runs the machinery and the cattle. Our son Daniel does the selling and the supermarket side. We've got eight full-time staff and up to forty seasonal workers in the summer and autumn for cutting and packing. Our daughter Grace works at a bank's customer service centre in the city.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. Daniel uses it to forecast how much we'll cut each week. I've used it to write the staff handbook and once to check a contract, because lawyers cost a fortune. I don't rely on it. I check what it says the same way I check a new cutter's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a tool like any other, and good businesses will use it sensibly. I'd say it at church coffee after the service, and at the growers' meeting, without making a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes, and I'm fine with that. The supermarket's still in charge of my week and the weather's still in charge of my year. AI doesn't change either of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let Daniel use it more for forecasting, if it helps him guess the orders better. Buy a new leek trimmer for the pack-house, about thirty thousand. Hire the seasonal crew the same way as always, mostly the same families who come back every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the same families come back every year. Tell me about them.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Novaks have been coming for eleven years, father, mother and now the two sons. They cut leeks faster than anyone I've ever seen. We have a barbecue for the crew at the end of the season, and Mrs Novak brings a cake that I've never managed to get the recipe for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever want AI to help with the supermarket orders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it could tell me at six in the morning what they'd cancel at four, I'd pay anything. But it can't read a buyer's mind any better than I can. The buyer probably doesn't know himself until his boss rings him.

S0.say: It's a tool like any other, and good businesses will use it sensibly. I'd say that at church coffee and at the growers' meeting without making a fuss.
S0.think: Nothing changes, and I'm fine with that. The supermarket is still in charge of my week and the weather is still in charge of my year.
S0.do: Lets her son Daniel use AI more for forecasting cutting volumes. Buys a new leek trimmer for the pack-house at about thirty thousand and hires the usual seasonal families.
S0.quote: The supermarket's still in charge of my week and the weather's still in charge of my year.
S0.fieldNote: Sara is practical and proud of the family business, which runs to a supermarket's daily orders. Her loyalty to the returning seasonal families is warm and specific. Her frustration is with buyers who cancel late, not with technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow change is how business should work: try it, prove it, then use it. Hiring fewer young people is a mistake, but I'd rather firms chose that than the government forcing them to hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's fine for us. The slow bit suits me, I like to see a thing work on someone else's farm first. What worries me is that the supermarkets would use it before we do. Their buyers would have better forecasts than us and squeeze us harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay for Daniel to go on a course about the new forecasting tools, around two thousand, so we're not behind the supermarket. Take on two school leavers as apprentices in the pack-house, because if firms aren't hiring them, we'd better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slightly uneasy about the supermarket getting cleverer. Otherwise calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you take on apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what you do in a community. My father took on lads from the estate when nobody else would, and two of them ended up running farms. If firms stop hiring young people, families like ours should step in, not wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it look like if the supermarket's forecasts were better than yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd know before I did that my carrots were going to be short, and they'd have already lined up another grower. I'd find out when the order dropped. That's not a fair fight, but it's their right to do it, I suppose.

S1.say: Slow change is how business should work: try it, prove it, then use it. Hiring fewer young people is a mistake, but I'd rather firms chose that than the government forcing them.
S1.think: The slow pace suits me because I like to see things work elsewhere first. What worries me is the supermarkets using it first, getting better forecasts and squeezing us harder.
S1.do: Pays about two thousand for her son's course on forecasting tools so they keep up with the supermarket. Takes on two school leavers as apprentices in the pack-house.
S1.feel: Slightly uneasy about the supermarket getting cleverer, otherwise calm.
S1.quote: My father took on lads from the estate when nobody else would, and two of them ended up running farms.
S1.fieldNote: Her traditional values come through as duty: families and businesses should step in before government. She sees the risk clearly but accepts the supermarket's right to use better tools. Her father's example guides her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say business will adjust and people will find new work, like they always have. The politicians shouting about it should calm down and let things settle. And I'd say people should look after their families, not wait for a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's Grace. She works in customer service at a bank, answering calls and emails. That's exactly the routine office work on the card. She's twenty-nine, she's renting, and she's got her heart set on buying a flat next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ring Grace and tell her there's a job in the family business if she needs one, doing the office side, which is a mess. Help her with the deposit if her job goes, maybe twenty thousand. Use an assistant for our own office paperwork once Daniel's tested it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for Grace. Sort of pleased, too, if I'm honest, because I'd love her back in the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Grace on the phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to pray about it, and then to ring me back. And that she's always been good with people, which no computer is. She'd say Mum, I'm not coming home to sort out invoices. And I'd say, the invoices need sorting, love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should look after their families and not wait for a handout. Is that what you're doing for Grace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, exactly. That's how it should work. Not everyone has a family business to fall back on, I know that. But for us, family comes first, then church, then the government, if you need it at all.

S2.say: Business will adjust and people will find new work, like they always have. Politicians shouting should calm down, and people should look after their families, not wait for a handout.
S2.think: It's Grace I'd worry about. Her bank customer service job is exactly the routine office work on the card, and she's twenty-nine, renting and hoping to buy a flat next year.
S2.do: Offers her daughter Grace a job running the family business office. Sets aside about twenty thousand to help with a flat deposit if her job goes, and uses an assistant for farm paperwork once Daniel has tested it.
S2.feel: Anxious for her daughter, and a little pleased at the thought of having her back in the business.
S2.quote: She'd say Mum, I'm not coming home to sort out invoices. And I'd say, the invoices need sorting, love.
S2.fieldNote: Her answer to the threat is family first, then church, then government only if needed. She accepts gently that not everyone has a family business behind them. Hope and worry about her daughter sit together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who built this have earned something, but they should give back, through charities and local projects, like the wealthy used to. Taxing everyone more isn't the answer. It drives the good businesses away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this one wouldn't hurt us. Physical work is untouched, and people still eat vegetables. If anything, the well-off would buy more of the expensive stuff, the tenderstem broccoli and the baby leeks. But I'd be watching Grace and the church families who work in offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grow more of the premium lines for the supermarket, maybe fifty more acres of tenderstem. Keep the seasonal crew as they are. Give more to the church hardship fund, maybe five thousand, because some of the families there would be in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. We'd be doing well while people we pray with are losing their jobs. That's not comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at church would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Bakers. He's an accountant and she does payroll for a big firm. Both thinking jobs, both on that card, three teenagers. If they both went at once, they'd lose the house. I'd want the church to be there before they had to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said tax isn't the answer. What if charity isn't enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd accept something, I suppose, but tied to work. Pay firms to take people on, not pay people to stay at home. I don't want to see the Bakers on benefits. I want to see them working.

S3.say: The people who built this have earned something, but they should give back through charities and local projects. Taxing everyone more isn't the answer, because it drives good businesses away.
S3.think: This one wouldn't hurt us, since people still eat vegetables and the well-off would buy more premium lines. But I'd be watching Grace and the church families who work in offices.
S3.do: Grows about fifty more acres of premium tenderstem broccoli for the supermarket and keeps the seasonal crew. Gives around five thousand more to the church hardship fund.
S3.feel: Uneasy at doing well while people she prays with lose their jobs.
S3.quote: We'd be doing well while people we pray with are losing their jobs. That's not comfortable.
S3.fieldNote: Her faith community is where she sees the crisis land. Pushed on whether charity is enough, she concedes support tied to work, which fits her views. She'd act through the church before anyone has to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in vegetables have been coming for years, and good businesses will use them. But the families who've worked for us deserve to be treated right through it. That's my responsibility, not the government's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd want them. Half the summer I'm short of cutters, and I've lost crops because I couldn't get them picked. If a robot can cut broccoli, I'd have one tomorrow. But the Novaks would be out of work, and that sits badly with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wait to see one working on another grower's farm, then lease two cutting robots in the second half of the year, maybe sixty thousand. Keep the Novaks for the jobs robots can't do yet, like the leeks. Talk to Mr Novak straight about what's coming, before he hears it somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved and sad at the same time. Relieved about the labour, sad about the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Novak?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he's welcome as long as there's work, and that I'd give him a good reference anywhere. And that maybe his sons should learn to fix the robots, because someone will have to. He'd probably laugh and say the robots can't cut leeks like him. For a few years, he'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You worried most about Grace earlier. This one, you're relieved. Is that what you expected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I thought robots would be the one that frightened me. But I've been short of hands for ten years. What frightens me is the supermarket using robots too, to grow their own, and not needing us at all.

S4.say: Robots in vegetables have been coming for years, and good businesses will use them. But the families who've worked for us deserve to be treated right, and that's my responsibility, not the government's.
S4.think: I'd want them, because half the summer I'm short of cutters and I've lost crops I couldn't get picked. But the Novaks would be out of work, and that sits badly with me.
S4.do: Waits to see robots working on another grower's farm, then leases two cutting robots for about sixty thousand in the second half of the year. Keeps the Novaks on leeks and tells Mr Novak directly what's coming.
S4.feel: Relieved about labour and sad about the people, and newly worried the supermarket might grow its own with robots.
S4.quote: He'd probably laugh and say the robots can't cut leeks like him. For a few years, he'd be right.
S4.fieldNote: She surprised herself: the robot picture brings relief because she's been short of labour for a decade. The real fear turns out to be the supermarket cutting growers out entirely. Her sense of duty to the Novak family stays strong.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, but not for the reason I expected. The supermarkets could grow their own with robots and not need us. What would help is fair contracts, so they can't cancel orders the afternoon before, and a level playing field so family growers aren't squeezed out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the waste. Every picture, nobody talked about the veg we throw away because a buyer changed his mind. If AI could stop that, it would be the best thing it ever did. Feeding cabbages to cattle because a spreadsheet changed is a sin.

headlineQuote: Feeding cabbages to cattle because a spreadsheet changed is a sin.
portrait: Sara Walsh is fifty-eight and grows leeks, cabbages, broccoli and carrots for two supermarkets with her husband Pete and son Daniel, plus a big seasonal crew. She uses AI now and then and waits to see things work elsewhere. Her views are traditional and pro-market: family first, then church, then government only if needed. She worries first about the supermarket getting cleverer and then about her daughter Grace's bank job and families at church. The robot picture surprised her with relief, because she's been short of cutters for years, until she realised the supermarkets might grow their own and cut growers out.
biggestWorry: The robots picture, because supermarkets could grow their own vegetables with robots and stop needing family growers.
whatWouldHelp: Fair contracts that stop supermarkets cancelling orders the afternoon before, and a level playing field for family growers.
